summary.text:
Rural Scottish unitary with a £401.4m external debt book forecast at 31 March 2026 (PWLB fixed £387.4m plus a small LOBO position of £14.0m — the LOBO runs down £5m during 2025/26 as at least one call/maturity lands). Capital Financing Requirement is £546.8m at revised 2025/26, up £24.6m from the original TMSS. Balance-sheet identity ties exactly at every reference date: CFR less other long-term liabilities less external debt equals the printed under-borrowing figure (£38.5m at 31 March 2026 revised; £50.6m at 31 March 2025 actual). Average investment balance during H1 2025/26 was £52.2m and the paper states £nil core cash available for more than one year, so the internal borrowing position is genuinely running against day-to-day liquidity.

The most substantial disclosure is the IFRS 16 restatement. Section 4 spells out that the 3 High Schools PPP was revalued adding £31.2m to reported external debt, and the paper walks through the consequent revisions to the Authorised Limit (£663.5m to £720.4m), Operational Boundary (£530.8m to £600.3m) and CFR (£522.2m to £546.8m). Financing costs to net revenue steps from 8.0% to 9.2% in the same movement — attributable, per the paper, to the same accounting change. The paper's second unusual feature is a '50-year target %' line drawn on the PWLB rates chart (page 17), stepping up from around 4.68% to around 5.20% in early September; the 50-year certainty rate ran at 5.83% average and finished at 5.98%, so the trigger was not tripped and no long-dated borrowing was taken on that basis.

No loan-book reconciliation was possible. The paper prints PWLB debt only as an aggregate (£387.4m forecast, £330.0m actual) with no portfolio weighted rate or loan count, and our bc-loans file's start-date column for Scottish Borders is unreliable enough that the as-at filter returns zero for every historic date tested. The unfiltered aggregate (54 loans, £384,355,495, 4.5883% weighted) sits within £3m of their year-end forecast but the reference dates cannot be lined up. Recorded as a file gap; the email does not quote either figure.

officer.body:
Hi Lizzie,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Mid-Year Report 2025/26 that went to Council on 4 December. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report is one of the cleaner IFRS 16 walkthroughs we've read this year and this is offered in that spirit.

The reason we say that is section 4. Most mid-year reports we've read mention IFRS 16 in passing, if at all. Yours puts the £31.2m PPP revaluation on the three High Schools next to the revised indicators and lets the reader see where the movement came from — Authorised Limit up £56.9m to £720.4m, Operational Boundary up £69.5m to £600.3m, CFR up £24.6m to £546.8m, with the Other Long-Term Liabilities line carrying £36.0m of that in one step. The ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue moves from 8.0% to 9.2% in the same walkthrough, which lines up with the sentence on page 9 that says reported financing costs increased as a result. That is a very clean audit trail for a member picking the paper up cold, and it's the kind of disclosure we can compare directly across the councils we've read.

The second thing that caught the eye is the '50-year target %' line on the PWLB rates chart on page 17. Reading from the axis it looks to sit around 4.68% through the first four months of the half and step up to around 5.20% in early September. The 50-year certainty rate averaged 5.83% and finished at 5.98%, so the trigger wasn't hit during H1 and the paper's own line about elevated yields at the 25-to-50-year end (page 16) is what it looks like on the chart. Of the councils we've read, only one other publishes a numeric long-end trigger of that kind, and moving it visibly in-year — rather than restating it once a year — is more active than most. We publish the 50-year certainty rate at both fixings each day and hold the history back to 2010, if that's useful for tracking against the target line. It's at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

One balance-sheet observation. Your under-borrowing sits at £38.5m at the revised year-end and averaged £52.2m of investments through the half, and the paper is explicit that you hold £nil core cash for more than one year. Net loans requirement is what's genuinely running against day-to-day liquidity rather than a treasury reserve — so the £30m of new external borrowing taken in H1 (page 16) is coming in against a book where the internal cushion isn't really there. We built a page (pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis) that runs the day's PWLB certainty and HRA curves against a user-loaded book, alongside the DMO premature-repayment curve. It might be useful when the next tranche is drawn, particularly if the shape of the maturity profile matters to how it lands against the liability benchmark.

One coverage note that belongs on our side rather than yours. We hold 54 PWLB loans for the Council in our own file totalling £384.4m and cannot cleanly reconcile that against the £387.4m forecast in your Table 4 because your paper prints only the aggregate and our file's drawdown-date column for the Council is not reliable enough to filter by date. Those figures aren't quoted in this email for that reason — we mention it only because it's a file-quality point for us to fix, not something we would ask you to help us with.

On the academy: four courses fit squarely — IFRS 16 and the prudential indicators, which is the section 4 walkthrough above; Liability benchmark and internal borrowing, which is the £38.5m under-borrowed / £52.2m average investment tension; The long-end of the PWLB curve, which is your 50-year target discipline; and PWLB break costs, which is the DMO repayment curve we referred to at the start. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you find any of it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Sources: Treasury Management Mid-Year Report 2025/26 (Appendix 1, doc 94995) and its covering report (doc 94994), both Scottish Borders Council, 4 December 2025.
